analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by the entire Florida House delegation, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from selling any leases to explore for or produce oil, natural gas, or other minerals in three areas off Florida: the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic up to the Georgia border [S2][S3]. It was introduced in July 2005 and referred to the House Resources Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities in Florida whose economies rest on beaches and tourism, commercial and recreational fishing interests, and residents who would face the risk of spills, drilling infrastructure, and onshore industrial support along the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. A permanent ban would also protect the coastline for future administrations that might otherwise sell leases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities, beach tourism, and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits the Interior Secretary from issuing leases for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or any other mineral in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic planning area to the Florida-Georgia border [S2][S3].

Because the prohibition is written directly into statute and overrides 'any other law' [S3], it would have been much harder for a future administration to open these waters to drilling than the temporary moratoria in place at the time.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential reserves in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic; the federal Treasury would forgo any lease bonuses, royalties, and taxes from future production in those areas.

drawbacks.text: Permanently placing the eastern Gulf and South Atlantic off limits forecloses domestic oil and gas development that could add to energy supply, and forgoes federal royalty revenue and jobs associated with offshore production.

A statutory ban is inflexible: if national energy needs changed sharply, Congress would have to pass new legislation to reopen any of the three planning areas, since the bill overrides conflicting laws [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Florida's coastline, the bill traded a permanent shield against spills and drilling infrastructure for forgone energy production and federal revenue. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs spill risk to beaches and fisheries against energy supply — but the bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh it at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee a week later, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Katherine Harris introduced the Florida Coastline Protection Act on July 12, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day [S5].
On July 20, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which is where the action record ends [S5].

The bill attracted 19 cosponsors — 15 Republicans and 4 Democrats [S4] — all Florida members, per the list of original cosigners in the bill text [S3], meaning the state's House delegation backed it across party lines.
No committee hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests are better off: the waters off Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts remained available for potential leasing, and no committee ever acted to block it. Florida's coastal communities got no added protection from the statute they asked their delegation to pass.

for.name: Katherine Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban offshore drilling off Florida's coast.

for.name: Florida House delegation members
for.role: 19 cosponsors (15 Republicans, 4 Democrats), including Mack, Miller of Florida, Bilirakis, Brown-Waite, the Diaz-Balarts, Foley, Keller, Ros-Lehtinen, Young, Shaw, Putnam, Crenshaw, Stearns, Hastings, Feeney, Wasserman Schultz, and Meek
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original signers when it was introduced.

against.name: House Committee on Resources leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing, chaired by a pro-drilling chairman in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat on the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Producers seeking access to federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico and South Atlantic
against.what_they_did: Supported continued leasing off Florida's coast during the 109th Congress's push to expand Gulf drilling.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was overwhelmingly bipartisan and regional rather than partisan: 15 Republican and 4 Democratic cosponsors, all from Florida's House delegation [S4][S3]; there is no recorded vote showing party lines because it never reached the floor [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have permanently barred leasing for oil, gas, and mineral exploration and production in the eastern Gulf, the Straits of Florida, and the South Atlantic [S2][S3], eliminating potential access to those federal waters. Because it died in committee, producers kept those areas open to future leasing.

industries.industry: Florida beach tourism and coastal hospitality
industries.note: A permanent drilling ban would protect the beaches that anchor the state's tourism economy from spills and offshore infrastructure. The industry's interest ran alongside coastal residents' interest in an unpolluted coastline.
Fisheries in the eastern Gulf and South Atlantic would face less risk of drilling-related contamination and platform disruption under a statutory ban [S2][S3].
